solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Head examination needs it

blocks.note: an oral is a spoken examination
'it' is an old euphemism for sex appeal or sex itself

explanation.surface: A doctor or phrenologist insists a proper head examination requires something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks anatomical, but it is slang for the act itself; ORAL is the spoken exam, and 'it' is the coy word for intercourse.
explanation.definitionFit: In vulgar slang, giving someone head means performing fellatio or cunnilingus on them.

clue.text: One mounting Cyclops's top grade, long 'beast'

indicators.note: in a down clue, to mount something is to climb up and sit above it, so this piece comes first in the column

blocks.note: 'an' means one, as in 'an apple'
the setter speaking of himself: Cyclops is = I'M
A is the highest exam grade
L is the abbreviation for long

explanation.surface: Someone climbing on the setter is called a top-grade, long beast, in a smutty Private Eye way.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by their pseudonym, so 'Cyclops's' is 'Cyclops is', I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: A beast is any living creature other than a human, which is what animal names.

clue.text: (& 22dn.) Extent of London's sources of cash injection typically, yet woefully slim with it?

definitions.note: the City (of London) gives the answer's first word, its limits its extent

indicators.note: a source is where something begins, so only the opening letter of each word counts
something done woefully is done badly, so these letters come out in a poor, jumbled order

blocks.note: the initials of four consecutive words
taken as written, into the anagram
taken as written, added to the anagram

explanation.surface: A dig at London's financial district, whose cash injections never seem to make it slim.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, the square mile, which fits the money in the surface; its limits are its boundaries.
explanation.definitionFit: City limits are the boundaries marking how far a town reaches, so they fix its geographical extent.

clue.text: Right side of your arse is big cold mass

indicators.note: the right-hand side of a written word is its tail, so only the closing letters are taken

blocks.note: the final two letters of the word
a crude anatomical synonym

explanation.surface: A schoolboy insult: the right side of your backside is a big cold mass.
explanation.walkthrough: The old schoolboy joke that the planet's name sounds like 'your anus' is built into the wordplay itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Uranus is an ice giant, the seventh planet, a huge frigid body of gas and ice far from the Sun.

clue.text: Porky Tory leader out of formal wear (replaced by Labour leader)

indicators.note: being out of something means removed from it, so one letter leaves the phrase
a replacement fills the vacated spot, so a new letter takes the departing one's place
the leader goes in front, so only the first letter of the party name is wanted

blocks.note: white tie is the most formal evening dress code
first letter, the one removed
first letter, the one put in

explanation.surface: A fat Tory leader squeezed out of his dinner suit and swapped for the Labour leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Porky' looks like an insult for a fat politician, but it is rhyming slang: porky pie = lie. Swap the T of WHITE TIE for L.
explanation.definitionFit: A porky is British rhyming-slang for an untruth, and a harmless or minor untruth is a white lie.

clue.text: Company 'C' surrounded by top show-off

indicators.note: whatever is surrounded sits inside a ring, so these letters go within another word

blocks.note: CO is the standard abbreviation for company
taken as written
the peak is the top of a mountain

explanation.surface: A firm called C finds itself hemmed in by a boastful boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like a description of the show-off as top dog, but it is the summit of a mountain; the quoted 'C' is just the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The male peafowl struts and fans its tail, so the bird's name is used figuratively for a vain, flamboyant person.

clue.text: (& 24dn/ 26ac.) Lead news is 'Stupid Tory Preston gaffe' – iron out

indicators.note: something put out is ejected, so these letters are struck from the rest
something stupid makes no sense, so the letters are scrambled into a new sensible order

blocks.note: taken as written
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: A tabloid splash about a Tory blunder in Preston, with the creases ironed out.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove F and E from the quoted headline, then rearrange the rest; 'iron out' reads as smoothing over but is FE removed.
explanation.definitionFit: The lead item in a newspaper is the article given top billing on its first sheet.

clue.text: Loose end activity? Oh dear, air needs refreshing!

indicators.note: to refresh something is to make it over anew, so the letters are reworked into a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone at a loose end discovers the room badly needs airing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose end' looks like idleness, but it is the rear end being loose.
explanation.definitionFit: The condition is literally the bowels running loosely, an activity of the backside, so the phrase is a cheeky cryptic description.

clue.text: House leader given the boot, a schmuck, ultimately a nerd

indicators.note: booting out the leader expels whoever is at the front, so the opening letter goes
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: a manor is a large country house
taken as written
the final letter of the Yiddish insult

explanation.surface: The Leader of the House is sacked and branded a schmuck and a nerd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House leader' suggests the Leader of the Commons; it is MANOR losing its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Anorak is British slang for an obsessive, socially awkward enthusiast, after the waterproof jackets worn by trainspotters.

clue.text: Not all 'bicycle men' cycling? Pity

indicators.note: taking not all of the phrase means only a stretch of its letters is used
to cycle is to go round, so letters from the front ride round to the back

blocks.note: the run of letters after the opening BI

explanation.surface: A pity that only some of the cyclists are actually out riding.
explanation.walkthrough: Take CYCLEMEN from the quoted phrase and move CY from the front to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Clemency is mercy or lenience shown to an offender, and pity in its sense of compassionate forbearance means the same.

clue.text: Bill lacking neckwear to strangle Corbyn's no.1

indicators.note: strangling means gripping round the throat, so one piece wraps around another
number one is the first in line, so only the opening letter is used

blocks.note: lacking a tie is having NO TIE
the initial of the former Labour leader's name

explanation.surface: A tieless Bill tries to throttle Jeremy Corbyn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name; it is a poster. Corbyn, famously tieless, was Labour leader at the time.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill is a printed sheet stuck up in public, such as a poster, which is exactly a posted public announcement.

clue.text: Casino employee gets wood meeting Brenda?

indicators.note: things that meet end up side by side, so these pieces are simply joined

blocks.note: deal is pine or fir timber
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A croupier gets aroused on meeting the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets wood' is crude slang for an erection, but 'wood' is deal timber. Private Eye always calls Elizabeth II 'Brenda'.
explanation.definitionFit: At a casino, the staff member who hands out cards at the gaming tables is called the dealer.

clue.text: Barking, Leeds, etc. to ditch political candidate

indicators.note: barking means barking mad, crazy, so the letters go wild into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Constituencies like Barking and Leeds are dropping their sitting candidates.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking looks like another place-name in the list (it is an east London constituency) but signals madness.
explanation.definitionFit: When a local party refuses to readopt its sitting MP or nominee for the next election, it is said to deselect them.

clue.text: Right engages in unfeeling terror

indicators.note: to engage in something is to get inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: the dead feel nothing
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: The political Right indulges in callous terror tactics.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes into DEAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Terror and dread are both synonyms for intense fear of something about to happen.

clue.text: MP behind ministers, one gambling on securing seat

indicators.note: to secure is to hold fast, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: one who backs a horse bets on it
a bench is a long seat

explanation.surface: An MP propping up the government is betting on keeping their seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Securing seat' reads as winning a constituency; it is BENCH held in BACKER.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Commons, MPs without government or shadow posts sit on the rows behind the front-bench ministers.

clue.text: Deplorable pap? Conclusion: one Times supplement

indicators.note: something deplorable is in a sorry state, so these letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
the end is the conclusion
Roman numeral for one
the multiplication sign

explanation.surface: A complaint that a Times supplement is nothing but deplorable mush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times supplement' suggests the newspaper's magazine; Times is the X sign and the capital is camouflage.
explanation.definitionFit: An appendix is extra material added at the back of a book, which is a supplement to the main text.

clue.text: Ex-Labour minister's to make a move on the board

definitions.text: to make a move on the board

blocks.note: first meaning: Barbara, a cabinet minister under Wilson and Callaghan

blocks.clueFragment: to make a move on the board
blocks.note: second meaning: the chess manoeuvre moving king and rook together

explanation.walkthrough: 'The board' suggests a company boardroom, but it is a chessboard. Barbara Castle was a leading Labour cabinet minister of the 1960s and 70s.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is the surname of a famous politician and also the chess verb for the king-and-rook move.

clue.text: May is at that point, since being rejected?

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so this word is turned round

blocks.note: there means at that place or point
as means since, in 'as it was late'

explanation.surface: Theresa May has been where she is ever since being rejected by voters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May' looks like the month or a verb; it is the then Prime Minister's surname, and the answer is her first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Theresa May was the British Prime Minister at the time, so her surname clues her forename by association.

clue.text: Trump's crown concerning – certainly not much of a hairstyle

indicators.note: the crown is the top of the head, and in a down clue the top letter is the first

blocks.note: the initial letter of the name
on means about or concerning
'sure' is an informal 'certainly'

explanation.surface: A jibe at Donald Trump's thinning crown and his famously odd hairdo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crown' is doubly apt: it selects the top letter, and a tonsure is shaved on the crown.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonsure is the shaved patch on top of a monk's head, so it is barely a haircut at all.

clue.text: Advantage of parliamentary figure getting clap from a number of people?

blocks.note: a whip is the party official who enforces voting discipline

blocks.clueFragment: clap from a number of people
blocks.note: a round of applause, as in 'give them a big hand'

explanation.surface: A parliamentary whip benefits from a burst of applause from the benches.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags 'clap' as applause from a crowd, not a single slap.
explanation.definitionFit: To have the whip hand is an idiom for holding control or the upper hand over someone.

clue.text: Sick of being unsuccessful? F-off!

indicators.note: taking something off removes it, so that letter is cut away

blocks.note: to fail is to be unsuccessful
the letter to be removed

explanation.surface: Someone fed up with failure tells the world to eff off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sick of' looks like weary of; 'Sick' is the definition and 'F-off' is a coy swear that strips the F from FAILING.
explanation.definitionFit: Ailing describes someone in poor health or unwell, which is what sick means as an adjective.

clue.text: Model knackered after sex? Hardly ever

indicators.note: knackered is British slang for worn out or broken, so the letters fall apart and are rebuilt
coming after something means following it, so this piece is placed second

blocks.note: sex shortened to its initial, as in form abbreviations
taken as written

explanation.surface: A model, worn out after sex, admits it happens hardly ever.
explanation.walkthrough: S then a rearranged MODEL; the abbreviation of sex to S is a loose one.
explanation.definitionFit: Both expressions describe something occurring rarely, on very few occasions; they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: see 3dn.
Lunar I's working place offering relief

indicators.note: something working is in motion, so these letters are set moving into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The working site of a lunar mission, Lunar I, is where relief is offered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relief' suggests aid or rescue for a space crew; it is relieving oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: Relieving oneself is a euphemism for urinating, and a urinal is the fixture for doing it.

clue.text: Smile awkwardly, being gobbled by Kitty, who'll not hesitate to give an opinion

definitions.text: who'll not hesitate to give an opinion

indicators.note: done awkwardly means clumsily, so these letters come out in a muddled order
whatever is gobbled ends up inside the eater, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: taken as written
the kitty or pot is the pool of money in a card game

explanation.surface: A woman named Kitty, never shy of an opinion, swallows an awkward grin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' looks like a person or a cat; it is the betting pot.
explanation.definitionFit: A polemist writes or speaks forceful, combative arguments, so they are someone quick to voice strong views.

clue.text: see 7ac.
Agent's thing produces pong – is A&E involved at the end?

indicators.note: involved means intricate and tangled, so these letters are wound into a new order
the end of a word is its final letter, which is all that is taken

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, ampersand dropped
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A secret agent's mysterious item gives off a stink; will a hospital casualty unit end up dealing with it?
explanation.walkthrough: A&E is Accident and Emergency, the British hospital casualty department. The end of 'the' supplies the last E.
explanation.definitionFit: Spying is the business of a secret agent, so espionage is the agent's line of work or 'thing'.

clue.text: see 7ac.
